title: Job 42:10–17
context: The narrator reports that the LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends and gave him twice as much as he had before, and that his brothers, sisters, and acquaintances came to eat with him and comfort him “concerning all the evil that the LORD had brought on him.” Job has seven sons and three daughters, names the daughters Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren Happuch, gives them an inheritance among their brothers, and lives to see four generations before he dies “old and full of days.” Both traditions read the restoration as the LORD’s free gift after the book has already resisted the retribution scheme (ch. 21; cf. 42:7), not as a formula that piety pays, and both hold that the new children do not replace or erase the children who died.

verses.text: The LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends. The LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends. The LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.” Arminian readers note that the restoration comes as the LORD’s gift, linked in time to Job’s prayer for others.

It is not presented as a payment for suffering.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s free grace in the restoration rather than a reward earned by Job.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse in light of the book’s earlier challenge to the retribution scheme (ch. 21), so that the ending shows God’s goodness rather than a prosperity formula.

verses.text: Then all his brothers, all his sisters, and all those who had been of his acquaintance before, came to him and ate bread with him in his house. They comforted him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that the LORD had brought on him. Everyone also gave him a piece of money, and everyone a ring of gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job’s brothers, sisters, and acquaintances “comforted him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that the LORD had brought on him.” Arminian readers note the return of the community that had been estranged (19:13–14).

They read “brought on him” alongside the prologue’s account of Satan’s role.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see comfort restored, and they read the phrase under God’s governing providence without making God the author of evil.

Shared ground: both traditions point to the discussion at Judges 9:23 and to Job’s confession in 1:21, rather than reopening the question here.

verses.text: So the LORD blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the LORD blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning.” Arminian readers note that the numbers listed are double those in 1:3.

The narrator presents the increase as the LORD’s blessing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s kindness in the latter end of Job’s life.

Shared ground: both traditions note the doubling carefully, and both caution against drawing from it a rule that suffering will always be repaid in material terms in this life.

verses.text: He had also seven sons and three daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He had also seven sons and three daughters.” Arminian readers note that the number matches the children named in 1:2.

Some suggest the number was not doubled because the first children were not lost to God, though this is an inference the text does not state.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise treat that suggestion as a possible, hedged reading.

Shared ground: both traditions read the new children as a real gift, while holding pastorally that they do not replace or erase the sons and daughters who died (1:18–19), whose loss remains part of Job’s story.

verses.text: He called the name of the first, Jemimah; and the name of the second, Keziah; and the name of the third, Keren Happuch.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He called the name of the first, Jemimah; and the name of the second, Keziah; and the name of the third, Keren Happuch.” Arminian readers note that the daughters are named while the sons are not.

The names are often linked to a dove, a fragrant spice, and a cosmetic, though these meanings are suggested rather than certain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the attention the narrator gives the daughters and hold the meaning of the names lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions see in the naming a sign of the delight and honor given to these daughters, without building doctrine on the possible meanings.

verses.text: In all the land were no women found so beautiful as the daughters of Job. Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.” Arminian readers note that the daughters share in the inheritance, which may have been unusual in a setting where sons normally inherited (cf. Num 27:8).

The narrator also notes their beauty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job’s generosity toward his daughters, reported plainly.

Shared ground: both traditions note the inheritance as a detail of Job’s restored household, without pressing it into a larger theory than the text supplies.

verses.text: After this Job lived one hundred forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, to four generations.
verses.arminianNotes:
“After this Job lived one hundred forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, to four generations.” Arminian readers note the long life and the generations Job lives to see.

The verse presents a full and settled old age.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s kindness in the length of Job’s days and the family around him.

Shared ground: both traditions read the long life as part of the LORD’s gift, not as proof that every faithful sufferer will live long.

verses.text: So Job died, being old and full of days.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So Job died, being old and full of days.” Arminian readers note that the phrase “old and full of days” is also used of Isaac (Gen 35:29).

The book closes with Job at peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a quiet close to Job’s story under God’s care.

Shared ground: both traditions read the ending as God’s freedom and goodness shown to Job, and some point to the perseverance of Job and the outcome named in James 5:11.
